reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (cold reader 2)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: I read CONTEXT whole (section 'When your voice is everybody else's voice', the paragraph that starts "Temporary Separation."), then DRAFT, SOURCE and the_change, and formed my verdict before opening ADMISSION.json. The draft is the paragraph's last sentence, "You want to be able to let the quiet little preferences that you have bubble up to the surface and know for sure that you’re not going by what your social group would want you to do." It sits once in CONTEXT, after "As you differentiate, you learn to tell which of those apply.", in place of "You want to let your quieter preferences bubble up to the surface so you can be sure you’re not just echoing your social group." It does what the_change says: Emulate's sentence, with no quote marks around "social". MEANING: SOURCE's two points are both here: quieter preferences surfacing ("quiet little preferences ... bubble up to the surface"), and being able to tell they are your own and not the group's ("know for sure that you’re not going by what your social group would want you to do", for his "tell your own signal from the social echo"). Soft spots I weighed and did not fail on: (1) "echoing your social group" became "going by what your social group would want you to do", which leans from repeating the group's voice toward following its wishes. The section covers both ("You don’t know what you want, until you have heard what someone else wants"; "neither in rebellion nor in compliance with others"), so it stays inside the section's idea and introduces no new fact. (2) "just" is gone from "not just echoing", so the claim reads a little more absolute, but the replaced words' "be sure" and the draft's "know for sure" assert the same certainty. (3) "quiet little" for "quieter" is warmer and smaller in feel, but it is the same preferences. (4) His "only long enough" is not in the replaced words and is not asked of this change, and the kept sentences before it carry the for-a-time versus long-term point. Nothing is added: no first-person claim, no named thing, no study (C03, C04 absent), and "your social group" is the "people or group" of the paragraph's first sentence (C02 clear). FIT: the sentence is wordier than the one it replaces ("that you have", "would want you to do") but in the register of its neighbours ("that you normally would get answers from"). It reads as a plain spoken sentence. The move from the paragraph's impersonal "it may be wise" to a direct "You want" is the same move the replaced sentence made, so the change adds no seam. TELL ROWS: none PRESENT. Closest calls: T22 (coach register): "You want to be able to" anticipates what the reader wants, but the sentence gives the reason for the separation (so quiet preferences can surface and be checked against the group), in the guide's own second-person voice used throughout this section, so I do not count it. T15 (humanizer rewording): it is a rewording of the replaced sentence on the same skeleton, but the phrases are plain spoken ones, not rare synonyms, and no other tell is carried over with it. T29: without this sentence the paragraph never says what the separation is for, so it is a new consideration and not a restatement. T21: the two coordinated goals (let preferences surface, check they are yours) are one purpose, as in the replaced sentence, and the linter raised no packed-sentence finding. T06: "bubble up to the surface" is the image the sentence already had. T13, T09 and T02: the paragraph's other sentences carry variation and entrenchment (some come back, some cannot), so it is not a bare slot list. The other rows are clear. LINTER: "D9 follows the source order" is accepted: a one-sentence change whose two points have a fixed order (surface, then check). "E36/E41 heavy second person" is accepted: 13.5 per 100 is the draft sentence alone (5 in 37 words); the replaced sentence was denser (5 in 24 words), the paragraph's other three sentences run about 8 per 100, and the whole section is addressed to "you" (the camp list, the questions, "Give your inner child..."), so the density is the section's norm, and the sentence has no scenery and is not reassurance alone. Bookkeeping, not a fail: the ledger's T14 and T15 lines say the sentence "puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped" and "puts back the author's words or meaning"; here nothing was put back (it is Emulate's sentence as it came, minus the quote marks), so that is template text. My own reading finds both rows absent for the reasons above.
